Have you tested the full function in context with the provided benchmarking tools? From a few personal spot checks, the change tended to make it worse (tested with Node, not Bun) - as holey arrays stay that way, and every read access will continue to be slower than a packed array.

I checked the actual read pattern. These arrays are only read in `mapAnalysisChunksToPreparedChunks`, which loops over `chunks.length` (1 in normal mode, one per \n in pre-wrap). 

Each iteration reads at most 3 slots from each array, so we're talking 3-6 total reads in the common case. The hole-check penalty on that few reads is negligible.

That said, after running the benchmarks  provided in this project, the allocation difference for arrays of size 10-120 is also negligible, so this change probably doesn't matter either way. Happy to close this PR.

AI-proposed optimizations always have to be taken with a grain of salt. It can find great optimizations, but the code may be very ugly to read. For me, it's more about what it attempted vs the end result. That's why I posted the results here as an issue for others to get inspired by (and not as a clear "hey, here you go, faster").

The models may also easily miss architectural changes that proper manual profiling may easily unveil.

For this pass, the auto-performance loop has been based on things I've seen have made real improvements from our own manual work: switching a parser with many closures into a class, caring about V8 internals, etc.. It's been interesting to see it applied to all sorts of code and how different architectures either benefit from it, or not at all.

I'm sure pretext will see many more improvements over the coming weeks and months.

I've done similar things before — directly reading fonts and then handling layout and rendering — but it introduces a lot more complexity, including but not limited to:

- Font Management: Network Loading & Caching

  Unlike the DOM, which has the browser's built-in font stack, you have to manage all fonts yourself. In real-world engineering, you also need to consider font file size (CJK fonts can easily range from several MB to tens of MB), on-demand loading (font subsetting or incremental font transfer), and coordinated loading of multiple font files. The complexity here is easily underestimated.

- Word Segmentation / Line Breaking

  Using ICU's line break algorithm to determine breakable points is the proper approach. Browsers do this internally as well. In JS environments, you can use a WASM-compiled version of ICU, or the browser-native Intl.Segmenter API (now supported by all major browsers). Beyond word segmentation, there's an often-overlooked aspect: bidi (bidirectional text). If you need to support mixed Arabic or Hebrew text, you'll also need to implement the Unicode Bidi Algorithm.

- Shaping

  opentype.js is mostly usable for simple scripts (Latin, CJK), but falls short with complex scripts. HarfBuzz WASM is currently the only truly reliable solution on the Web. The trade-off is a larger bundle size, but there's no substitute for correct shaping.
  
- Font Fallback

  This is the most easily overlooked yet extremely troublesome part. The font fallback logic that browsers handle for you is actually very complex: for each character, you need to determine whether the current font has the corresponding glyph, and if not, search through the fallback font chain by priority. Moreover, after splitting by fallback, each segment needs to be shaped independently (since different fonts have different GSUB/GPOS tables), then reassembled. In practice, you also have to deal with visual jumping caused by inconsistent metrics (ascender/descender/line height) across fallback fonts.

- Emoji Support

  The challenges exist on two levels: first, at the input level, emoji can be multi-codepoint ZWJ sequences, skin tone modifiers, flag sequences, etc., which require the shaping engine to correctly identify and process them; second, at the rendering level, emoji font formats (COLR/CPAL, CBDT, SVG-in-OpenType) are completely different from regular outline glyphs, requiring a separate rendering path.

To be honest, once you've done all of this, it's basically no different from rewriting the browser canvas's text API from scratch — it's just too hard😭. So for a library focused on typesetting, using the canvas API to abstract away the low-level details is a very efficient approach.

## Status update: all browser oracles green, synced with upstream

### What this PR does

Adds `wordBreak?: 'normal' | 'keep-all'` to `PrepareOptions` — `prepare(text, font, { wordBreak: 'keep-all' })` matches CSS `word-break: keep-all` for CJK text.

**How it works** (all changes in `src/layout.ts` `measureAnalysis()`):
1. Skip per-character CJK grapheme decomposition — segments stay word-level
2. Merge consecutive adjacent text segments that touch CJK into one unbreakable unit (handles Latin↔CJK boundaries without spaces)
3. Three guards keep the merge correct: non-word-like segments (em-dash, brackets) skip merge; word-terminating punctuation (。、,)」) ends the merge unit; Latin↔Latin boundaries are never merged
4. `breakableWidths` populated on merged segments for overflow-wrap grapheme fallback
5. New engine profile flag `preferFillBeforeGraphemeBreak` (true on Safari) to match Safari's fill-remaining-space behavior vs Chrome/Firefox flush-first

`layout()` hot path is unaffected. Non-CJK text is identical to `word-break: normal`.

### Current oracle results (post upstream sync through `9364741`)

| Oracle | Chrome | Safari |
|---|---|---|
| keep-all (17 cases) | 17/17 ✅ | 17/17 ✅ |
| pre-wrap (15 cases) | 15/15 ✅ | 15/15 ✅ |

| Browser | Result | Break mismatches |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome | 17/17 ✅ | 0 (fully strict) |
| Safari | 17/17 ✅ | 4 (signatures match exactly) |

Chrome is now fully strict — a same-height break-position shift in Chrome will fail the oracle. Safari's 4 documented divergences pass only when the exact signature matches; if a divergence resolves or shifts, the oracle fails.

The 4 Safari divergences are all Chrome/spec-correct cases where Safari keeps CJK+punctuation runs together instead of breaking after `。` or at the em-dash:
- `cjk punctuation`: line 1 `世界。` vs `世界。新し`
- `cjk hyphen latin`: line 1 `日本語foo-` vs `日本語foo-b`
- `cjk em-dash cjk`: line 2 `—` vs `—テス`
- `kinsoku period`: line 2 `。` vs `。世界`

Pretext relies on canvas.font, which does not support font-variation-settings.
However, variable fonts can still work if their axes (like "wght") are mapped through standard font properties like font-weight.

For example:

ctx.font = '700 16px "InterVariable"';

If you're using font-variation-settings, it won’t affect measurement unless it's reflected in the font string.

A practical workaround is to encode variation axes into the font string before passing it to Pretext, and re-run prepare() whenever those values change.
